planting.note: Pruning group 2; an heirloom raised by the Jackman nursery in the 1870s, it flowers earliest on old wood and again lightly on new growth, so limit any hard pruning to right after the first flush. Can also be planted in fall.

directions: One of the older large-flowered heirlooms still in circulation, Daniel Deronda opens large, semi-double, violet-blue flowers with a paler central bar and creamy stamens in late spring, the early blooms often fuller than the later single flush that follows on new wood in summer. The semi-double effect comes from an extra layer of narrow inner petals that fades somewhat as the flowers age, giving a two-toned look to an established plant in full bloom. Grow it on a trellis or through an open shrub with its roots shaded and kept cool, and water deeply during dry spells since the heavier double flowers are thirstier than single-flowered types.

planting.note: Pruning group 3; a French-raised nineteenth-century heirloom that blooms entirely on new wood, so cut the whole plant back hard in late winter. Can also be planted in fall.

directions: A nineteenth-century French introduction still sought out by collectors, Madame Grange bears richly velvety, deep red-purple flowers with a faint darker bar and a contrasting cluster of pale stamens from midsummer into early fall. The thick, slightly twisted petals give the flowers a heavier, more substantial look than many later large-flowered hybrids, and the rich coloring holds well even in full summer heat. Because it flowers only on the current season's growth, cut the entire vine back to a low pair of buds in late winter, and train it onto a trellis or obelisk with the root zone shaded and mulched.

planting.note: Pruning group 2; flowers on old wood in late spring and again on new growth in late summer, so keep any shaping cuts light and timed right after the first flush. Can also be planted in fall.

directions: An old-fashioned large-flowered hybrid, Mrs Hope produces broad, pale lavender-blue flowers with a deeper mauve-pink central bar down each petal and a prominent boss of reddish stamens, opening in late spring and again lightly in late summer. The pale coloring is most vivid on younger growth and softens slightly as flowers age, giving a two-toned display across an established plant. Train it onto a trellis, arch, or obelisk with its roots cool and shaded, water deeply during dry spells, and avoid hard pruning since the best early bloom comes from wood made the previous year.

planting.note: Pruning group 3; a modern large-flowered hybrid from the Guernsey breeding program that blooms on new wood from midsummer on, so cut back hard in late winter. Can also be planted in fall.

directions: A compact, modern large-flowered hybrid from the Guernsey Clematis breeding program, The Vagabond opens rich purple-red flowers with a narrow lighter pink margin along each petal edge, the contrast sharpest on the earliest buds of the season and softening somewhat in high heat. Its shorter, more restrained habit compared to older large-flowered hybrids suits a large container or a small trellis near a patio as easily as a mixed border. Grow in full sun with roots shaded and cool, and cut the whole plant back to a low pair of healthy buds in late winter since bloom comes entirely on the current season's growth.

planting.note: Pruning group 3; like other viticella types it flowers only on new wood, so cut the whole plant back hard in late winter. Can also be planted in fall.

directions: Among the darkest of the viticella-group clematis, Black Prince opens small, nodding, velvety flowers in a near-black deep plum-purple that catches the light with a subtle sheen, carried in great profusion from midsummer into early fall. Like other viticella selections it is naturally resistant to clematis wilt and tolerates a harder annual cutback better than most large-flowered hybrids, making it forgiving for less experienced gardeners. Train it through a dark-foliaged shrub or over a low fence where the intense coloring shows well against lighter backdrops, and water regularly through summer to keep the profuse bloom going.

planting.note: Pruning group 3; blooms on new wood only, so cut the whole plant back hard in late winter. Can also be planted in fall.

directions: A free-flowering viticella selection, Pink Fantasy covers itself in medium-sized, soft pink flowers brushed with a deeper rose-pink bar down the center of each petal, opening continuously from midsummer into early fall rather than in a single concentrated flush. Its relatively small, dainty flowers and light, airy habit make it a good choice for weaving through a pale-flowered shrub rose or over a low arch without overwhelming a companion plant. Being a viticella type, it shrugs off clematis wilt far better than many large-flowered hybrids, and an annual hard cutback in late winter keeps it compact and heavy-blooming.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; a non-vining, herbaceous clematis that can be grown in a mixed border without a climbing support.

directions: Bred from the herbaceous integrifolia line, Tapestry is a non-climbing clematis that forms a lax, self-supporting mound rather than a vine, producing nodding, bell-shaped flowers in a blend of dusky pink and soft purple with recurved petal tips from early summer into fall. Its sprawling habit is useful for weaving along the front of a border or draping over a low wall, something a true vining clematis cannot do without support. Because flowers form on new growth, cut the whole plant back close to the ground in late winter, and stake loosely if stems begin to flop under the weight of bloom.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; a compact, non-vining clematis bred from Baltic integrifolia lines that needs no climbing support.

directions: Part of a line of Baltic-bred integrifolia hybrids, Juuli grows as an upright, non-climbing clump rather than a vine, bearing nodding, bell-shaped violet-blue flowers with twisted, recurved petal tips over a long season from early summer into fall. Its sturdy, self-supporting stems make it well suited to the front of a sunny border or a large container without any trellis or stake. Cut the plant back close to the ground in late winter since blooms form entirely on new growth, and keep soil evenly moist through summer heat.

planting.note: Blooms on old wood, so prune only right after flowering if size control is needed (Group 1); give it a large, sturdy structure since it is among the most vigorous of the montana types.

directions: This long-grown, larger-flowered form of the species produces pure white blooms noticeably bigger than typical wild Clematis montana, smothering a mature plant in a single dense flush each spring and filling the air with a light vanilla-almond scent. Its exceptional vigor means it quickly outgrows a small trellis, so give it a large pergola, mature tree, or long fence to scramble across rather than a confined space. Because flowering happens entirely on the previous year's growth, any pruning needed to keep it in bounds should be done immediately after bloom, and the roots are best kept cool and shaded while the vine reaches into full sun above.

planting.note: Herbaceous scrambling type that blooms on new wood; cut hard back to the ground in late winter like a Group 3 clematis. Can also be planted in fall.

directions: An older hybrid of Clematis vitalba and C. heracleifolia, Praecox behaves as a sprawling, scrambling sub-shrub rather than a true climber, lacking the twining leaf stalks of vining types and needing to be tied to a low support or allowed to spill over a wall. From late summer it bears masses of small, faintly scented, pale blue-white flowers with recurved sepals, opening somewhat earlier in the season than its better-known relative 'Mrs Robert Brydon'. Its non-climbing habit and ground-covering spread make it useful at the front of a large border, and cutting the whole plant back hard in late winter keeps new growth dense and floriferous.

common_name: Wyevale Tube Clematis (Non-Vining Blue Shrub Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; a non-vining, sub-shrubby clematis that needs no climbing support, though floppy stems benefit from discreet staking.

directions: A selection of the tube clematis valued for deeper coloring than the wild species, Wyevale forms a rounded, non-climbing sub-shrub of coarse, deeply veined leaves topped from late summer into fall by clusters of small, tubular, hyacinth-scented flowers in rich violet-blue with recurved tips. The woody base persists through winter even as the upper stems die back, so cut old flowering stems down to the framework in late winter rather than to the ground. Its sprawling, somewhat lax habit benefits from discreet staking or the support of neighboring shrubs, and it rewards average garden soil with reliable, late-season bloom when little else in the border is flowering.

planting.note: Blooms on old wood in spring; prune lightly right after flowering only to shape (Group 1), since hard pruning removes next year's flowering wood.

directions: A fully double form of the small-flowered macropetala group, White Moth opens nodding, lantern-shaped blooms packed with narrow, pure white inner petals in mid spring, giving a fluffier, more intricate look than the single-flowered species. Like other macropetala types it is fully hardy and blooms earliest of any clematis group, making a welcome display on a fence or low trellis before most other vines have leafed out. Prune only lightly right after the spring flush to remove dead wood, since next year's blooms form on wood made this season, and the attractive silvery seed heads that follow are worth leaving in place through summer.

planting.note: Blooms on old wood in spring; prune lightly right after flowering only to shape (Group 1), since hard pruning removes next year's flowering wood.

directions: A Scandinavian-raised macropetala selection prized for extra cold hardiness, Jan Lindmark bears nodding, semi-double, lilac-purple lantern flowers in mid spring with the characteristic extra inner petaloid staminodes typical of the group. Being a macropetala type, it tolerates far colder winters than most large-flowered hybrids and flowers earliest of any clematis in the garden, well before deciduous vines have fully leafed out. Give it only light shaping right after the spring bloom, since flowers form on wood grown the previous year, and let the fluffy silver seed heads stand through the summer for added interest.

planting.note: Blooms on old wood in spring; prune lightly right after flowering only to shape (Group 1), since hard pruning removes next year's flowering wood.

directions: An American-raised macropetala selection, Rosy O'Grady opens nodding, bell-shaped flowers in clear pink with a paler center and the group's characteristic extra feathery inner petals, blooming in mid spring on a compact vine well suited to a mailbox post, low fence, or large container trellis. Its soft pink coloring stands apart from the typical blues and purples of most macropetala cultivars, and like its relatives it is extremely cold hardy and flowers earlier in the season than almost any other clematis type. Shape it only lightly right after flowering, since next year's buds form on this year's growth, and the silvery seed heads that follow extend its appeal well past bloom time.

planting.note: Blooms on old wood in spring; prune lightly right after flowering only to shape (Group 1), since hard pruning removes next year's flowering wood.

directions: A compact alpina cultivar grown for its unusually soft coloring, Willy produces small, nodding, bell-shaped flowers in pale pink shading to near-white at the petal edges, opening in mid spring on slender stems that twine through a low trellis or shrub without overwhelming it. Like other alpina types it needs no hard pruning and flowers earliest of any clematis group, making it a reliable early-season companion planted through spring-flowering shrubs such as forsythia. Prune only lightly right after bloom to remove dead growth and keep it tidy, since flower buds form on the current season's wood for the following spring.

planting.note: Blooms on old wood in spring; prune lightly right after flowering only to shape (Group 1), since hard pruning removes next year's flowering wood.

directions: Named for its resemblance to the nodding spurred flowers of the garden perennial it borrows its name from, this alpina selection bears pale, powdery blue, bell-shaped blooms with a lighter center in mid spring on a slender, twining vine well suited to a low trellis or large container. Its gentle coloring and compact scale make it a natural choice near a shaded entryway or underplanted with spring bulbs that finish blooming around the same time. Being fully hardy and blooming earliest of any clematis group, it needs only light pruning right after flowering to remove dead wood, since buds for next spring form on this year's growth.

planting.note: Blooms on old wood in spring; prune lightly right after flowering only to shape (Group 1), since hard pruning removes next year's flowering wood.

directions: A soft-colored alpina cultivar, Pink Flamingo opens nodding, lantern-shaped flowers in pale candy pink that deepens slightly toward the petal tips, blooming in mid spring on slim, twining stems suited to a low fence, obelisk, or large container. The understated pink reads well against a dark fence or evergreen backdrop, and its small scale makes it easy to tuck into a tight space where a larger vine would be unwelcome. Like other alpina types it flowers earliest of any clematis group and needs only light pruning right after bloom, since the fluffy seed heads that follow extend seasonal interest well into summer.
